stem: A client who can become pregnant is starting isotretinoin and says, “I am not sexually active, so the iPLEDGE pregnancy-prevention requirements do not apply to me.” Which response is most accurate in August 2026?

options.A: Continuous abstinence moves the client out of the iPLEDGE group that can become pregnant, so enrollment and pretreatment pregnancy testing are not required while abstinence continues.
options.B: Continuous abstinence can be used instead of two contraceptive methods, but the client still remains in iPLEDGE and must complete the required pregnancy testing, including pretreatment tests in a medical setting.
options.C: The client may enroll in iPLEDGE but can defer pregnancy testing until treatment begins, because pretreatment testing is intended for clients who are using contraceptive methods.
options.D: The client can postpone iPLEDGE enrollment until sexual activity begins, then complete pregnancy testing before the next isotretinoin prescription is dispensed.

rationale: Current isotretinoin labeling states that patients who can become pregnant must enroll in and comply with the iPLEDGE REMS, including pregnancy-testing and pregnancy-prevention requirements. The labeling allows continuous abstinence from sexual contact that could result in pregnancy as an alternative to using two simultaneous contraceptive methods, but abstinence does not remove the patient from the iPLEDGE category or eliminate pregnancy testing. Current labeling requires two negative pretreatment pregnancy tests in a medical setting and pregnancy testing during and after treatment. FDA's June 16, 2026 update states that implementation of the February 2026 iPLEDGE modifications was delayed from August 8 to November 15, 2026 and that, until implementation is complete, FDA continues its pregnancy-testing enforcement discretion; FDA also states that pretreatment pregnancy tests must continue to be completed in a medical setting. Therefore B is correct. A incorrectly treats abstinence as changing reproductive-status classification and eliminating enrollment/testing. C delays required pretreatment testing. D delays required enrollment and testing until sexual activity begins even though the REMS applies based on the ability to become pregnant, not current sexual activity.
educational_objective: For isotretinoin, teach patients who can become pregnant that continuous abstinence may satisfy the pregnancy-prevention alternative to two contraceptive methods, but it does not remove iPLEDGE enrollment or required pregnancy testing, including pretreatment testing in a medical setting.
source_organization: U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA); U.S. National Library of Medicine — DailyMed
source_document_title: iPLEDGE Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS); Isotretinoin Capsules — Full Prescribing Information
source_version_date: FDA iPLEDGE page updated June 16, 2026; current isotretinoin DailyMed labeling dated July 2026; both accessed 2026-08-25
source_locator: FDA iPLEDGE REMS > Implementation for iPLEDGE REMS Modifications Delayed Until November (June 16, 2026): planned implementation moved from August 8 to November 15, 2026; until full implementation FDA continues pregnancy-testing enforcement discretion described in the October 2023 update. FDA February 9, 2026 update: pretreatment pregnancy tests must continue in a medical setting; if permitted by the prescriber, pregnancy tests during and after treatment may be completed outside a medical setting. DailyMed Isotretinoin Capsules §5.2 iPLEDGE REMS: patients who can become pregnant must enroll and comply with pregnancy-testing and pregnancy-prevention requirements. §8.3 Females and Males of Reproductive Potential: pretreatment pregnancy testing is required; two forms of contraception are not required if the patient commits to continuous abstinence from sexual contact that may result in pregnancy.
source_claim_supported: In August 2026, iPLEDGE remains in effect. Patients who can become pregnant remain subject to enrollment and pregnancy-testing requirements even if they choose continuous abstinence; abstinence is an alternative to two contraceptive methods, not an exemption from the REMS or pretreatment testing.

supporting_sources.organization: U.S. National Library of Medicine — DailyMed
supporting_sources.locator: §5.2 iPLEDGE REMS: patients who can become pregnant must be enrolled and comply with pregnancy testing/prevention. §8.3 Pregnancy Testing: testing is required prior to, during and after treatment; pretreatment screening and confirmatory tests are completed in a medical setting. §8.3 Contraception: two contraceptive methods are not required when the patient commits to continuous abstinence from sexual contact that may result in pregnancy.
supporting_sources.claim_supported: Current product labeling directly supports continued iPLEDGE enrollment/testing for patients who can become pregnant and identifies continuous abstinence as an alternative pregnancy-prevention strategy rather than a program exemption.

correction_summary: Rebuilt all four responses with parallel capitalization and comparable clinical detail, removing distractor-only absolute wording. The revised keyed answer distinguishes continuous abstinence as an allowed pregnancy-prevention strategy from the separate, continuing requirements for iPLEDGE enrollment and pregnancy testing, while preserving the August 2026 implementation status of FDA-approved REMS modifications.

audit_findings.clinical_category: Isotretinoin medication safety — iPLEDGE pregnancy prevention and testing
audit_findings.stem: PASS — identifies a patient who can become pregnant, a clear abstinence misconception, and the August 2026 timing needed to account for the delayed iPLEDGE modification implementation.
audit_findings.option_A: PASS as distractor — continuous abstinence is an accepted pregnancy-prevention pathway, but it does not change the patient's reproductive-status classification or remove REMS enrollment and pregnancy-testing obligations.
audit_findings.option_B: PASS — directly reflects current FDA and DailyMed requirements: abstinence may replace two contraceptive methods, while enrollment and required pregnancy testing remain; uniquely best.
audit_findings.option_C: PASS as distractor — enrollment is appropriate, but current FDA guidance specifically preserves pretreatment pregnancy testing in a medical setting and does not permit deferring it until after treatment begins.
audit_findings.option_D: PASS as distractor — current sexual activity does not determine whether a patient who can become pregnant must enroll in iPLEDGE; delaying enrollment/testing until sexual activity begins conflicts with the REMS.
audit_findings.ambiguity: PASS — B is the only response that correctly separates pregnancy-prevention method choice from enrollment and testing obligations while remaining accurate for August 2026.
audit_findings.second_answer: EXCLUDED — A incorrectly removes REMS requirements, C delays pretreatment testing, and D delays enrollment/testing based on sexual activity.
audit_findings.cueing: PASS — all alternatives are substantive and similarly structured; capitalization is consistent and no distractor-only absolute term remains. B is somewhat longer because it must distinguish two separate requirements, but the alternatives contain comparable conditional detail and do not make length a reliable answer cue.
audit_findings.blueprint: PASS — NCSBN Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies includes medication-safety requirements, contraindication/risk review, and client medication education.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: PASS — challenged whether the February 2026 modifications or abstinence could eliminate testing or enrollment. FDA explicitly delayed implementation to November 15, 2026 and states pretreatment tests remain in a medical setting; current isotretinoin labeling separately requires REMS enrollment/testing for patients who can become pregnant and permits abstinence only as an alternative to two contraceptive methods. B remains uniquely correct.
